passage:
Ivan stood at the window of his Warsaw student flat, holding a vape he'd told himself was "just for exam weeks". That had been true once. Now it was the first thing he reached for after lectures, and the thing he reached for when the flat felt too quiet. "I can stop anytime," he'd said to himself again this morning.

That evening Beatriz, a friend from his course, noticed his hands shaking slightly at the café. "You've missed two labs," she said gently.

Ivan opened his notes app and counted honestly: missed labs, money spent, the mornings he felt flat. He read the list out loud, slowly.

"I think I need help," he said. Beatriz nodded. "The university health service does this. I'll come with you if you want."

Ivan booked it that night.

qa.q: What was Ivan holding at the window?
qa.a: Ivan was holding a vape he'd told himself was just for exam weeks.

qa.q: What is Ivan worried about or hiding from himself, and what shifts once the cost is counted?
qa.a: He kept saying he could stop anytime, but counting the missed labs, money and flat mornings honestly made him say he needed help.

qa.q: What would you advise Ivan to do next?
qa.a: Keep the appointment with the university health service, keep telling Beatriz, and avoid hiding it or calling it stress relief. 🤍

qa.q: How might Beatriz see Ivan's situation?
qa.a: Beatriz saw shaking hands and two missed labs and spoke gently instead of accusing, showing concern for a friend and offering to go along.

grounding: Ivan's occasional habit has become his way of coping and he says he can stop anytime, until he counts the cost, tells a friend and seeks help.

passage:
First week of term. Tushar played online matches on Friday nights with the hostel group. It was fun, loud, harmless.

Sixth week. Exams were close and his father's shop was struggling. Now he logged in every night after dinner and didn't stop until four. When Sarika asked why he looked grey in class, he said, "It's how I relax. I can quit whenever." He'd missed two lab submissions.

Ninth week, a Sunday. He sat on his bed and wrote on the back of a notice: missed labs, skipped meals, no calls home, three weeks of four-hour sleep. He stared at it for a long time. Then he walked to Sarika's room and showed her. "I don't think I can stop on my own." She went with him the next morning to the student counselling centre, and waited outside.

qa.q: On which nights did Tushar play in the first week of term?
qa.a: Tushar played online matches on Friday nights.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he stared at his list?
qa.a: Tushar felt shaken and worried, seeing in writing how much the gaming was costing him.

qa.q: What steps helped Tushar, and why?
qa.a: Counting the real cost honestly, telling Sarika, and going to the counselling centre early helped, because hiding it as relaxation was not working.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when Tushar showed her the list?
qa.a: Sarika probably felt worried but also relieved that he finally trusted her, which is why she went with him the next morning.

grounding: The three beats show a young man whose gaming becomes his way of coping, who counts the cost, tells a friend and seeks professional help early.

passage:
Yash, come, sit. You think your aunt was always this boring person who drinks only tea? At twenty-one, in my first job in the city, I started having a drink after work with colleagues. Just Fridays. Then after every hard day. Then alone, in my rented room, because it made the evenings quieter. I told myself it was stress relief. I told my sister I could stop anytime. I didn't.

One morning I missed a client meeting and couldn't remember the night before. I was frightened, Yash. Really frightened.

That week I did the hardest thing. I told my sister the whole truth, and she came with me to a doctor. I went to a support group every Thursday for two years.

So when you tell me your nightly vaping is just to calm down, I hear myself. I'm not angry. I'm asking you to look at the cost honestly.

qa.q: What happened on the morning that frightened the aunt?
qa.a: She missed a client meeting and couldn't remember the night before.

qa.q: What was the aunt feeling as a young woman when she kept saying she could stop?
qa.a: She was in denial and ashamed to admit the truth, telling herself the drinking was just stress relief.

qa.q: What turning point in the aunt's story made recovery possible?
qa.a: Telling her sister the whole truth and going to a doctor that week, then attending a support group, turned things around.

qa.q: How might the aunt's sister have felt when she heard the truth?
qa.a: The sister likely felt worried and shocked, but also trusted enough to go with her to the doctor.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young woman whose drinking became her way of coping, who admits it, tells someone safe and seeks professional help.
